name: Bessemer air conversion
summary: Blowing air through molten pig iron burned out carbon and supplied its own heat, turning iron into steel quickly and cheaply; it spread widely before being superseded.
description: Air blown through molten pig iron in a converter; oxidation supplies heat during conversion to steel.
tier_reason: Bulk air-conversion steelmaking enabled successive infrastructure, transport and manufacturing applications; the ranked referent is the production process.

date.basis: Patent year specified in the Science Museum collection record; not the date of universal commercial reliability.

events.statement: Air blown through molten pig iron in a converter; oxidation supplies heat during conversion to steel.
events.caveats: The object page is retrospective. Its separate compressed statement about later improvements is not used.

evidence.locator: Object 1869-41, description paragraph beginning Sir Henry Bessemer

date.label: by October 1858
date.basis: Göransson’s producer account, quoted in Bishop, reports the works already using the process by October 1858.

events.statement: By October 1858 Göransson reported that his firm was using the Bessemer method in its works to make steel.
events.population: Edsken/Högbo ironworks employees and steel producers in Sweden
events.caveats: Contemporary self-report is preserved through a later Smithsonian history. It gives an upper bound, not the first sale, and does not prove all variations used identical equipment.

evidence.supports: Reproduces the October 1858 producer account that the firm’s works were engaged in Bessemer steelmaking.

date.label: 1889–1890 census year
date.basis: The 1890 census period ran from July 1889 through June 1890.

events.statement: The U.S. census counted 51 Bessemer steel establishments in its 1890 period, compared with 11 in 1880.
events.scope: Bessemer steel works equipped with air converters, including the cited converter variants.
events.population: U.S. Bessemer steel establishments counted by the census
events.caveats: The count concerns establishments in the census, not necessarily simultaneous active converters; the 1890 definition includes named variants and is not a worldwide count.

evidence.supports: The report counts 11 U.S. Bessemer establishments in 1880 and 51 in the 1890 census period, including certain converter variants in the latter count.

date.basis: The source reports annual output for both calendar years.

events.statement: Reported U.S. Bessemer raw-steel output fell from 2,548,000 short tons in 1954 to 278,000 short tons in 1966.
events.scope: U.S. Bessemer raw-steel production in the reported industry series.
events.population: U.S. steel producers in the reported industry series
events.caveats: The table excludes foundries normally producing only steel castings. These two endpoints do not imply a monotonic decline or global cessation; 1967 combines Bessemer with open hearth.

evidence.supports: U.S. Bessemer raw-steel production was 2,548 thousand short tons in 1954 and 278 thousand in 1966; 1967 is combined with open hearth.

date.basis: The museum dates decommissioning and county history the final blow-out to 1974.

events.statement: The last Moss Bay Bessemer converter was blown out in 1974; Sheffield Museums describes its preserved Workington converter as the UK’s last working example.
events.scope: British Steel Corporation Bessemer converter at Workington.
events.caveats: This endpoint is limited to the Workington converter and the museum’s UK claim. Other steel production and rail rolling continued locally; no worldwide end is asserted.

evidence.supports: The museum says its Workington converter was decommissioned in 1974 and was the last working example in the UK.
The local history reports the last Moss Bay converter blown out in 1974, distinguishing later steelworks and rail rolling.

links.statement: Did steam blowing engines make the Bessemer blast practical? This would join steam to steel.
links.caveats: Evidence needed: Works descriptions naming the blowing engine in the specified Bessemer configuration.
links.finding: The documented Soho rotative engine initially drove a corn mill; the Bessemer record describes an air blast. Neither inspected source establishes that this named Soho engine or its design powered the specified Bessemer works; generic steam blowing cannot supply the missing link.

unresolved.note: The Workington and UK converter endpoint is local; worldwide end of air-converter steelmaking has not been established.
